You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: In MVFA's few-shot inference, the released code min-max normalises the zero-shot (text) branch and the few-shot (memory-bank) branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set and adds them with a fixed weight of 0.5, so the score of one image depends on the rest of the test set and a single incoming image cannot be scored. Can this transductive normalisation be replaced by an inductive one computed only from the K normal support images, at a small cost in AUROC? The inductive normaliser maps each branch's patch scores through the 1st and 99th percentiles of the leave-one-out patch scores of the supports (every patch of support i scored against the memory bank of the other K-1 supports and against the text anchors), which gives thousands of reference values even at K = 2; the fusion weight and the max pooling of the image score are kept fixed. Primary outcome: image-level and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive normalisation on each held-out BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the original method's AUROC across random half-size test subsets and at shifted prevalence (10% and 50% abnormal). Secondary outcome: sensitivity at 95% specificity with a threshold fixed from the support scores alone.
Rationale: The code check turned L10 into a sharper limitation (C1): the fusion is computed with test-set extremes, which makes the method non-deployable on a stream of images and makes its numbers depend on test-set composition; L8 adds that only threshold-free AUROC is reported, so this dependence stays invisible. Related work changes representations, prompts and fusion layers (LaRP-CLIP [57], HeadCLIP [17], ClipMPCAD [62]) but evaluates with the same AUROC; QueCo [56] even builds its reference from the unlabelled test set, while CANOR [30] shows that a few calibration scalars can be fitted cheaply for a frozen CLIP. The study is positioned as an evaluation-validity study with a simple inductive fix: it reuses the K normal supports MVFA already loads, needs no retraining, is confined to test_few.py, and runs on checkpoints retrained under the shared protocol. Keeping the pooling fixed isolates one component, and the inductive normaliser can be adopted by other methods evaluated on BMAD.

Review: Framed as an evaluation-validity study with an inductive fix, it targets a practice the CLIP anomaly-detection literature has not examined ([17], [56], [57]); the fix itself (normalising by reference statistics) is standard. Feedback: Show whether other BMAD baselines share the transductive normalisation; that would make the finding broader than MVFA.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- L8. Evaluation is limited to ROC AUC: no Dice/IoU, PRO/AUPRO, boundary metrics, lesion-level sensitivity, PR-AUC, sensitivity/specificity at a clinically chosen threshold, or calibration are reported. Pixel-level AUC pools all pixels and is dominated by abundant background, so a model that over-segments can still score 97-99% and the small AS gains cannot be interpreted as better localization; the near-ceiling values also leave almost no dynamic range for comparing methods. For classification, AUC says nothing about the operating point or whether the probability-like scores are calibrated, so the clinical usability of the outputs is unassessed.
- L10. The test-time fusion is under-specified: the paper never states whether the few-shot memory-bank branch is active in the zero-shot folds (where no target-domain references exist), never reports zero-only/few-only/fused scores separately, and sums a softmax probability with a cosine distance at fixed 0.5/0.5 weights without scale calibration. The final prediction is defined as a fixed 0.5/0.5 mixture of the two branches, but the few-shot branch requires labeled images from the same modality/anatomy as the test sample, which contradicts the zero-shot definition; if it is disabled the published formula does not apply to the zero-shot tables, and if it is populated with source normals the 'zero-shot' label is misleading. Because the two branches live on different scales and no branch-wise ablation is given, the contribution of each component to the headline numbers cannot be assessed and the zero-shot results cannot be reproduced from the text. Code check (released MVFA code): The released code shows what the paper leaves open: each branch's maps are min-max normalised with the minimum and maximum over the ENTIRE TEST SET and then fused with a fixed weight of 0.5 (see C1).
- L30. The anomaly-classification scoring pipeline is ambiguous: the paper never specifies which softmax class is scored, over which axis the maximum is taken, or how the binary label is encoded for the BCE loss. The zero-shot AC score is written as a max over G of a two-class softmax and the BCE target is the symbol c, so different readings (max over spatial positions of the anomalous-class probability vs max over classes) give different scores and calibrations. Because AUC is rank-based this does not by itself invalidate the reported numbers, but it prevents exact reproduction and interpretation of the anomaly scores shown qualitatively. Code check (released MVFA code): In the released code the image score on datasets with masks is the MAX of the fused pixel map; on datasets without masks it is the test-set-normalised, mean-pooled detection score; training mean-pools the detection map.
- L38. Image-level classification is computed as the maximum over spatial locations of the minimum distance to the normal memory bank, so a single outlier patch determines the image score, and this pooling choice is never compared with alternatives. The few-shot AC score takes max_G of a per-patch nearest-normal distance, coupling the global classification task to the most anomalous local region; the paper never compares max with mean or top-k aggregation, nor states whether the text branch uses the same pooling, so the contribution of the 'global' classification branch cannot be isolated. On datasets with large normal anatomy or noisy segmentation this can inflate AC independently of true image-level abnormality. Code check (released MVFA code): Confirmed in the released code for datasets with masks: the image score is the max over the fused pixel map, so a single spurious pixel can decide the label.
- C1. Scores are normalised with statistics of the whole test set: Before the two branches are fused, each branch's maps are min-max normalised using the minimum and maximum over the ENTIRE TEST SET, then combined with a fixed weight of 0.5. This normalisation is transductive: it cannot score a single incoming image, and the fused score of an image changes with the composition (prevalence, outliers) of the rest of the test set.
- C3. Paper and code disagree on image-level pooling: Eq. (3) of the paper defines the image-level loss with a max over the h x w anomaly map, while the released code mean-pools. Results in the paper therefore cannot be attributed to the method as described, and the effect of the pooling choice on detection is unknown.
Constraints:
- The problem will be investigated by a student team in the next few weeks by modifying the public code of the target paper (https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD) and evaluating on the public BMAD benchmark (brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT: RESC and OCT17, chest X-ray, histopathology), using a single Google Colab Pro GPU (A100 40GB or L4 24GB). No new clinical data can be collected and no new expert annotations can be made.
- Shared evaluation protocol (from the limitation group 'Leakage-free generalisation protocol': L1, L2, L11, L20, L22, L27, L37, C2): checkpoints and hyper-parameters are selected on a held-out validation split of the SOURCE modalities and never on the target test set, and the MVFA baseline is re-run under the same rule; results are reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and with a simple supervised baseline trained on the same labelled images (L31) where relevant.
